slides.1.title: The Tradition and Science of Vinho Verde's Light Sparkle
slides.1.html:
The light sparkle (Pétillant) of Vinho Verde is not added deliberately, but is a natural result of traditional winemaking.

🔬 Where the Light Sparkle Comes From

  • Traditional Vinho Verde finishes fermentation in stainless steel tanks and does not undergo malolactic fermentation (MLF)
  • Some CO₂ (a by-product of the conversion of malic acid to lactic acid) is retained in the wine
  • Pressure is usually only 1–2 bar (about 6 bar for traditional-method Champagne), with fine, short-lived bubbles
  • After opening, the bubbles disperse quickly, leaving a "prickle" rather than obvious bubbles

📅 Historical Background

  • Historically the wines of north-west Portugal were considered "too harsh" because of their high acidity
  • When farmers drank young Vinho Verde, the naturally retained CO₂ made it fresher and more refreshing
  • This "flaw" gradually became Vinho Verde's signature trait

🌿 Modern Trend: Still Alvarinho

  • Top Alvarinho producers in Monção/Melgaço (such as Soalheiro) increasingly make still versions
  • The aim is to let tasters focus on Alvarinho's varietal character rather than have their perception affected by the light sparkle
  • This reflects the market's recognition of Alvarinho as a serious fine white wine
slides.2.title: Pétillant Naturel (Pét-Nat): The Sparkling Revolution of Natural Wine
slides.2.html:
Pétillant Naturel (French for "naturally lightly sparkling"), abbreviated Pét-Nat, is the most closely watched sparkling wine style in the global natural wine movement.

🔬 How Pét-Nat Is Made

  • The grape juice is bottled before fermentation has fully finished (Méthode Ancestrale)
  • Yeast remaining in the bottle continues to consume residual sugar, producing CO₂ that forms the bubbles
  • There is only one fermentation (the traditional method has two), the oldest way of making sparkling wine
  • No sugar is added (liqueur de tirage) and there is no disgorgement (dégorgement); the wine is simply bottled

🌿 Characteristics of Pét-Nat

  • Usually with a little sediment (yeast cells), giving a slightly cloudy appearance
  • Irregular bubbles, livelier and lighter than the traditional method
  • Flavour: bready yeast notes, fresh fruit, natural and lively, often slightly sweet (if fermentation is not complete)
  • Alcohol is usually lower (10–12%), suited to everyday drinking

🇵🇹 Portuguese Pét-Nat Examples

  • Anselmo Mendes (Vinho Verde): a pioneer of top Alvarinho Pét-Nat
  • Niepoort Nat Cool: Pét-Nat by natural wine master Dirk Niepoort, made from Douro white varieties
  • Aphros (Vinho Verde): biodynamic Pét-Nat, a rising star of the fine natural wine market
slides.3.question: What process mainly gives traditional Vinho Verde its light sparkle (Pétillant)?
slides.3.options.0: The winemaker injecting CO₂ by hand before bottling
slides.3.options.1: Secondary fermentation in bottle by the traditional method
slides.3.options.2: Traditionally, CO₂ as a by-product of malolactic fermentation (MLF) (today mostly injected directly)
slides.3.options.3: The use of a special sparkling grape variety
slides.3.explanation: Vinho Verde's light sparkle is a natural result of traditional winemaking: traditionally the wine's malolactic fermentation (MLF) was delayed until after bottling, producing a little CO₂ in the bottle; today most producers inject CO₂ directly, at pressure below 1 bar. It was not a deliberately created sparkle but a centuries-old "flaw" of tradition that later became Vinho Verde's signature.
slides.4.question: What is the most fundamental production difference between Pétillant Naturel (Pét-Nat) and the traditional method (Método Clássico)?
slides.4.options.0: Pét-Nat uses more expensive grape varieties
slides.4.options.1: Pét-Nat has only one fermentation (completed in the bottle), while the traditional method has two (with sugar and yeast added for the second fermentation)
slides.4.options.3: Pét-Nat must have the lees removed, while the traditional method may keep them
slides.4.explanation: Pét-Nat uses the ancestral method (Méthode Ancestrale): the wine is bottled before fermentation has fully finished, and the yeast remaining in the bottle continues to produce CO₂, so there is only one fermentation throughout. The traditional method has two fermentations (after the first is complete, a "tirage liqueur" is added for secondary fermentation in bottle) and requires final disgorgement (dégorgement). Pét-Nat is more natural and older.
